How many frames a move remains active (can hurt opponents) for. For projectiles with a maximum active period, a value may be listed in [brackets], but this number is not factored into the move's total frame count.
For multi-hit moves with no gaps between the active hitboxes, active frames are listed as X,Y (or sometimes X*Y)

For multi-hit moves with gaps between hits, active frames are listed as X(n)Y where n = the frame gap between hitboxes.

Available options for canceling one move into another move.
"Chn": Chain cancel (Light normals; specific chain options listed in Description)

"TC": Target Combo

"Sp": Special move

"SA": Super Art (if a number is listed, refers only to that specific Super; SA3 = Lv.3 Super Art)

"Jmp": Jump cancel (usually on hit only, if applicable)

"SS": Serenity Stream (Chun-Li's stance)

"PS": Prowler Stance (Alex's stance)
If one hit of a multi-hit attack is cancelable, this can be indicated with (1st), (2nd), etc.

Occasionally, a move can be canceled only into a specific follow-up (e.g. Dee Jay [4]6P > 22PP); this can be indicated by listing the move input in the Cancel field, or with an asterisk that is explained in the move notes (Sp*)

Hitconfirm reaction windows into Special Moves, Target Combos, and Super Arts.
Refers to the amount of time (in frames) you have to cancel one attack into another attack on reaction
e.g. most cancelable 2MKs have a 13 frame window to cancel into a Special/Super on reaction, making them nearly impossible to hitconfirm

Counts from the first frame the attack connects until the final cancelable frame
Visual effects like hitsparks and HP drain do not actually occur until frame 2; the first frame is still counted to keep the numbers consistent with previous games, and because it is technically possible to start reacting to the character's reeling animation on frame 1

If a Target Combo is cancelable into another attack, the hitconfirm window will include the entire sequence starting from the first hit
If there is a frame gap on block between hits of the TC, the hitconfirm window may also be included for just the followup hit

Some sequences like Ken's 5MP~HP TC may have a range of values listed (43f~47f). In this example, inputting 5MP~HP at its usual timing gives a 43f hitconfirm into a Special/Super. Delaying the chain into HP gives more total time for the final hitconfirm.

Attack damage on hit. Multi-hit moves may have the damage listed for individual hits as X,Y (or sometimes X*Y). Sometimes a move's damage changes depending on which active frame connects, or on cinematic vs. non-cinematic hits; in this case, multiple values may be listed, and it will be clarified in the move description.

Some moves cause additional damage scaling in combos. Refer to Game Data page for a more detailed breakdown.
Scaling Types:

Starter: When a move begins the combo , the next attack is scaled by X percent
e.g. Ryu 2MK (20% Starter) > Hadoken: Hadoken is at 80% damage scaling

Combo: When a move is comboed into , the next attack is scaled by X percent or X number of hits
e.g. Ryu 2HP > OD High Blade Kick (2-Hit Combo Scaling) > Shoryuken: Shoryuken is at 70% damage scaling (100% > 100% > [skip 80%] > 70%)

e.g. Cammy 5HP > OD Spiral Arrow (5% Combo Scaling) > Cannon Spike: Cannon Spike is at 75% damage scaling (100% > 100% > [80-5 = 75%])

Immediate: When a move is comboed into , this attack is scaled by X percent
e.g. Drive Impact Crumple (20% Starter) > Throw (20% Immediate): Throw is at 60% damage scaling

Multiplier: A damage scaling multiplier applies after Perfect Parry (50%) and mid-combo Drive Rush (15%). Any hits in the combo continue their usual damage scaling, but reduced by these amounts. These can bring the minimum scaling below the usual 10%, and they stack with each other; as a result, the minimum scaling can reach 4% using a long Drive Rush combo after Perfect Parry.

Minimum Scaling: The lowest damage scaling that can be applied to an attack. Super Art Level 1/2/3 generally has 30%/40%/50% minimum scaling respectively. This ensures the attack will still do reasonable damage even at the end of a heavily scaled combo.

Refers to the frame advantage when canceling a normal, command normal, or Target Combo into Drive Rush on hit or block (abbreviated as DRC for Drive Rush Cancel). This is calculated at the moment a follow-up attack can be input, not at the moment the character can block or perform movement options. An attack that with DRC +8 on Hit can link into an 8-frame attack, and DRC +4 on Block can create a true blockstring into a 4-frame attack.
Note that any DRC on Block worse than +4 cannot form a true blockstring, allowing the opponent to interrupt with an invincible reversal. Most light normals are slightly negative after a DRC on block, meaning the opponent can mash their fastest normal to guarantee a counter-hit (though this requires fast reactions). The attacking character could punish this with Light > DRC into an immediate invincible attack, but this would be an incredibly expensive and high-risk gambit.

Most airborne command normals, special moves, and Super Arts put the user in a "Forced Knockdown" state. While in this state, an air knockdown will occur when being hit by any attack, even if it would otherwise cause an air reset.
As an example, Ryu's 2HP causes an air reset when used as an anti-air. Against a move like Cammy's Hooligan Combination, however, the 2HP puts her into an air knockdown state. This allows Ryu to successfully cancel 2HP into Shoryuken for a juggle, similar to how a Drive Impact wall splat works. Taking advantage of Forced Knockdown juggles is important for dealing with moves like Ken's Dragonlash, Dhalsim's Air Teleport, or Kimberly's 6HK~Hop sequence.

Moves that already cause an air knockdown, like most j.MP air-to-airs, will not display the "Forced Knockdown" message.

Refers to the direction an attack must be blocked. L is for Low attacks (must be blocked crouching), H is for High attacks/overheads (must be blocked standing), LH is for attacks that can be blocked crouching or standing. T is for Throw attacks which cannot be blocked.

When a character is put into an Air Knockdown state, it is often possible to follow up with a Juggle attack before they hit the ground. In the simplest terms, there are 2 main juggle states:
Free Juggle: any attack can juggle, causing an Air Reset or an Air Knockdown

Limited Juggle: only specific attacks with juggle potential may juggle

The following is a more detailed overview of the SF6 juggle system:

Juggle Count (JC) : The status of the character being juggled. A high JC limits which attacks can work in juggles.

JC0: free juggle state - any attack that can hit an airborne opponent will work

JC1+: limited juggle state - juggle only works if the attack's Juggle Limit ≥ defender's Juggle Count
A juggle count of -1 represents a crumple state; this can lead to a grounded or airborne hit depending on timing

Juggle Start (JS) : When starting a juggle, the opponent's JC will be set to this value. May be different vs. standing and airborne opponents.

Attack with Juggle Start value of 3 will put opponent at JC3, so only attacks with Juggle Limit value ≥ 3 can follow up

Even for attacks that don't normally start a juggle, this is relevant for Forced Knockdown and Crumple situations

Juggle Increase (JI) : When opponent is already in a juggle state, attacks will increase the opponent's JC by this amount.

Airborne opponent at JC1 followed by attack with Juggle Increase value of 3 will set opponent to JC4

Juggle Limit (JL) : Property of an attack hitbox that determines whether it connects on a juggled opponent. The JL must be ≥ the opponent's JC to hit successfully.

An uppercut with a JL value of 5 will connect on an opponent at JC5 or below, but will whiff on JC6 opponent

Most normals have a JL value of 0, meaning they only work in Free Juggle (JC0) states

Some multi-hit attacks have different JL values on each hit, so a 3-hit move may only hit twice in juggles

An example to tie everything together:

An attack (JS3) launches opponent into the air (Opponent now at JC3)

Followed up with an attack (JI2/JL4); it connects, because JL4 ≥ JC3 (Opponent now at JC5)

Attempts to juggle again with same attack (JL4), but whiffs because JL4 < JC5 (Opponent hits the ground)

Drive Rush notes:

DR normals have a Juggle Start/Increase value of 0

DR normals have +3 added to their usual Juggle Limit

More recently, the official definitions used by Capcom are slightly different than these community-designated terms. When reading official patch notes, the following terms are used instead:

Combo Count Initial Value

Combo Count Additional Value

Combo Count Upper Limit

These are frame advantage values when the attack hits or is blocked. If the number is positive, then the move will recover before the defender can act again. If the number is negative, the defender will be able to act before the attacker and maybe even punish. KD refers to knockdown on hit, and the listed KD Advantage refers to how many frames the attacker can act before the defender finishes their wakeup animation.
Note that generally, there is an extra +2 hit advantage on Counterhits and +4 hit advantage on Punish Counters (exceptions are noted in the description).

How many frames it takes for a move to finish after the active frames have finished. For projectiles, recovery is considered to begin after the first active frame.
Moves with different recovery values on hit/block/whiff may have multiple values listed like X(Y), with specific details listed in the description.

How many frames it takes before the move becomes 'active' or have a hit box. The last startup frame and the first active frame are the same frame, meaning all values are written as Startup + 1.
Moves with multiple relevant startup values may be listed as X(Y); for example, a move that hits airborne first before hitting grounded opponents, or a 2-hit move where the first hit whiffs at some ranges.

Some moves play out an extended recovery animation when no other button/direction is input (for crouching moves, it applies when holding any down direction). These are often referred to as "actionable recovery" frames; in some games, the term IASA (Interruptible As Soon As) refers to the frame that Actionable Recovery begins.
Letting the Actionable Recovery frames play out can change the character's position, potentially setting up spacing traps by recovering farther away. For example, Manon 5HP will recover much farther away from the opponent if no input is performed immediately after her recovery; holding back or down-back to block will keep her much closer to the opponent.

Introduction

edit

The successor of Shiranui-style ninja arts. A charming kunoichi who is as dedicated to love as she is to training. Loves cooking, Japanese dressmaking, flower arrangement, and traditional Japanese dance.

Gliding onto the stage with the elegance of a butterfly, Mai Shiranui plays as a midrange monster with a particular emphasis on tricky projectile mixups and a unique resource-based install. While Mai's kit can fly high, she's also a very straightforward and easily accessible character.

Mai's big claim to fame is her stellar neutral control. She has an arsenal of incredibly good buttons, chief (keef) among them her 5MP and 5HP. Her excellent 4HK anti-air doubles as a strong meaty pressure tool, and her 6MP overhead comes with all the standard benefits. In general, Mai has all the things a strong SF6 character wants in terms of buttons, but she really comes into her own with her special moves. Kachousen is one of the best fireballs in the game, thanks to the huge amount of utility packed into one move. Its uncharged variant is a decent projectile, but when charged up (or used with the OD variation) it bounces above the opponent on contact and falls onto them for an additional hit. If Mai is close, she can enforce a true high/low mixup by timing a strike alongside the fan fall, hitting them where it hurts the most. She also has a classic DP in Hishou Ryuuenjin, which lets her set up a mean zoning game if the opponent fails to stop her.

Kachousen's excellence informs the rest of Mai's kit, as the rest of her moves are all about getting the opponent nice and comfortable in the corner. Once she's ducked her way past the opponent's blows and found a hit, Mai's combos all give great corner carry thanks to Hissatsu Shinobi Bachi. Ryuuenbu is a disjointed poking special that's great for both counterpoking and setting up meaties, while Musasabi no Mai is an incredibly good divekick that causes Mai to hesitate before she launches downwards, which can easily mess up anti-air timings. Once the opponent is cornered, Mai uses Kachousen, the Drive System, her strong arsenal of pressure tools and her throw loop to break opponents down and send them packing. This is all standard shoto stuff, but what really lets Mai turn up the heat on her opponents is Kagerou no Mai, her install super.

Upon performing her Level 1, Mai gains Flame Stocks that enhance her special moves. Not only do all of her special moves gain better properties, but many of them also change their frame data. For example, Kachousen is much more advantaged on block, with charged flame Kachousen being very difficult to interrupt with a reversal. This gives Mai unique decision-making compared to the rest of the cast- does she spend Level 1 for a more consistent gameplan, but with less guaranteed return, or save for a Level 3 and be more dependent on the Drive System to enforce her offense? Mai's average damage is much lower than her contemporaries without Flame Stocks, meaning she has to make a very careful choice based on her opponent's life, her available Super meter, and even what round the match is currently on. Different matchups and situations call for different decisions, which gives Mai a lot to think about while she's running circles around her opponents.

Mai does have drawbacks, however. Her level one Super can work as an anti-air reversal, but it's not strike or projectile immune, limiting her options in the corner and especially in burnout. Her fan pressure is suffocating, but uncharged unenhanced Kachousen loses to strikes, forcing her to charge them in fireball wars and putting her at risk for jump ins. And worse yet, she has few ways outside of Kachousen to generate plus frames, and lacks Ken's close-range blender to keep the pressure going. Her DP is reliable, but it has terrible horizontal range and can be baited and punished with crafty spacing. Flame stocks are a powerful resource, but she has limited ways to combo into Kagerou no Mai, and without it her damage on big finishers suffers.

To sum it all up, Mai's strong zoning and potent Flame Stocks allow her to control the neutral like few else on the roster. Her simple, strong kit gives her a lot of ways to play around with the opponent, while also rewarding strong fundamentals consistently. If you prize a consistent partner and don't juggling resources a bit more than normal, there's few else who can put on a show quite like Mai.

Pick if you like:
Avoid if you dislike:

Fan Favorite: A zoning game that can be converted into a strong offense when executed correctly.

Deadly and Graceful: Great damage or corner carry routes, both of which are accessible from most hits.

Dangerous Beauty: Easy-to-manage multipurpose normal moves.

The Fire Gets Hotter: A snowballing mechanic with stock-enhanced specials.

Coming in Waves: Committing to your fireball game to apply pressure safely.

No Heat Without Fire: Lacking large damage cash outs without access to empowered specials.

Driven to Perfection: Lacking plus frames on block without Drive Rush.

The Dance Exhausts: Only has invincible level 2 and 3 supers, limiting her options on the back foot.

For multi-hit moves with gaps between hits, active frames are listed as X(n)Y where n = the frame gap between hitboxes.

Cancel

Available options for canceling one move into another move.
"Chn": Chain cancel (Light normals; specific chain options listed in Description)

"TC": Target Combo

"Sp": Special move

"SA": Super Art (if a number is listed, refers only to that specific Super; SA3 = Lv.3 Super Art)

"Jmp": Jump cancel (usually on hit only, if applicable)

"SS": Serenity Stream (Chun-Li's stance)

"PS": Prowler Stance (Alex's stance)
If one hit of a multi-hit attack is cancelable, this can be indicated with (1st), (2nd), etc.

Occasionally, a move can be canceled only into a specific follow-up (e.g. Dee Jay [4]6P > 22PP); this can be indicated by listing the move input in the Cancel field, or with an asterisk that is explained in the move notes (Sp*)

Cancel Hitconfirm Windows

Hitconfirm reaction windows into Special Moves, Target Combos, and Super Arts.
Refers to the amount of time (in frames) you have to cancel one attack into another attack on reaction
e.g. most cancelable 2MKs have a 13 frame window to cancel into a Special/Super on reaction, making them nearly impossible to hitconfirm

Counts from the first frame the attack connects until the final cancelable frame
Visual effects like hitsparks and HP drain do not actually occur until frame 2; the first frame is still counted to keep the numbers consistent with previous games, and because it is technically possible to start reacting to the character's reeling animation on frame 1

If a Target Combo is cancelable into another attack, the hitconfirm window will include the entire sequence starting from the first hit
If there is a frame gap on block between hits of the TC, the hitconfirm window may also be included for just the followup hit

Some sequences like Ken's 5MP~HP TC may have a range of values listed (43f~47f). In this example, inputting 5MP~HP at its usual timing gives a 43f hitconfirm into a Special/Super. Delaying the chain into HP gives more total time for the final hitconfirm.

Damage

Attack damage on hit. Multi-hit moves may have the damage listed for individual hits as X,Y (or sometimes X*Y). Sometimes a move's damage changes depending on which active frame connects, or on cinematic vs. non-cinematic hits; in this case, multiple values may be listed, and it will be clarified in the move description.

Damage Scaling

Some moves cause additional damage scaling in combos. Refer to Game Data page for a more detailed breakdown.
Scaling Types:

Starter: When a move begins the combo , the next attack is scaled by X percent
e.g. Ryu 2MK (20% Starter) > Hadoken: Hadoken is at 80% damage scaling

Combo: When a move is comboed into , the next attack is scaled by X percent or X number of hits
e.g. Ryu 2HP > OD High Blade Kick (2-Hit Combo Scaling) > Shoryuken: Shoryuken is at 70% damage scaling (100% > 100% > [skip 80%] > 70%)

e.g. Cammy 5HP > OD Spiral Arrow (5% Combo Scaling) > Cannon Spike: Cannon Spike is at 75% damage scaling (100% > 100% > [80-5 = 75%])

Immediate: When a move is comboed into , this attack is scaled by X percent
e.g. Drive Impact Crumple (20% Starter) > Throw (20% Immediate): Throw is at 60% damage scaling

Multiplier: A damage scaling multiplier applies after Perfect Parry (50%) and mid-combo Drive Rush (15%). Any hits in the combo continue their usual damage scaling, but reduced by these amounts. These can bring the minimum scaling below the usual 10%, and they stack with each other; as a result, the minimum scaling can reach 4% using a long Drive Rush combo after Perfect Parry.

Minimum Scaling: The lowest damage scaling that can be applied to an attack. Super Art Level 1/2/3 generally has 30%/40%/50% minimum scaling respectively. This ensures the attack will still do reasonable damage even at the end of a heavily scaled combo.

Drive Rush Cancel Advantage

Refers to the frame advantage when canceling a normal, command normal, or Target Combo into Drive Rush on hit or block (abbreviated as DRC for Drive Rush Cancel). This is calculated at the moment a follow-up attack can be input, not at the moment the character can block or perform movement options. An attack that with DRC +8 on Hit can link into an 8-frame attack, and DRC +4 on Block can create a true blockstring into a 4-frame attack.
Note that any DRC on Block worse than +4 cannot form a true blockstring, allowing the opponent to interrupt with an invincible reversal. Most light normals are slightly negative after a DRC on block, meaning the opponent can mash their fastest normal to guarantee a counter-hit (though this requires fast reactions). The attacking character could punish this with Light > DRC into an immediate invincible attack, but this would be an incredibly expensive and high-risk gambit.

Forced Knockdown

Most airborne command normals, special moves, and Super Arts put the user in a "Forced Knockdown" state. While in this state, an air knockdown will occur when being hit by any attack, even if it would otherwise cause an air reset.
As an example, Ryu's 2HP causes an air reset when used as an anti-air. Against a move like Cammy's Hooligan Combination, however, the 2HP puts her into an air knockdown state. This allows Ryu to successfully cancel 2HP into Shoryuken for a juggle, similar to how a Drive Impact wall splat works. Taking advantage of Forced Knockdown juggles is important for dealing with moves like Ken's Dragonlash, Dhalsim's Air Teleport, or Kimberly's 6HK~Hop sequence.

Moves that already cause an air knockdown, like most j.MP air-to-airs, will not display the "Forced Knockdown" message.

Guard

Refers to the direction an attack must be blocked. L is for Low attacks (must be blocked crouching), H is for High attacks/overheads (must be blocked standing), LH is for attacks that can be blocked crouching or standing. T is for Throw attacks which cannot be blocked.

Juggles

When a character is put into an Air Knockdown state, it is often possible to follow up with a Juggle attack before they hit the ground. In the simplest terms, there are 2 main juggle states:
Free Juggle: any attack can juggle, causing an Air Reset or an Air Knockdown

Limited Juggle: only specific attacks with juggle potential may juggle

The following is a more detailed overview of the SF6 juggle system:

Juggle Count (JC) : The status of the character being juggled. A high JC limits which attacks can work in juggles.

JC0: free juggle state - any attack that can hit an airborne opponent will work

JC1+: limited juggle state - juggle only works if the attack's Juggle Limit ≥ defender's Juggle Count
A juggle count of -1 represents a crumple state; this can lead to a grounded or airborne hit depending on timing

Juggle Start (JS) : When starting a juggle, the opponent's JC will be set to this value. May be different vs. standing and airborne opponents.

Attack with Juggle Start value of 3 will put opponent at JC3, so only attacks with Juggle Limit value ≥ 3 can follow up

Even for attacks that don't normally start a juggle, this is relevant for Forced Knockdown and Crumple situations

Juggle Increase (JI) : When opponent is already in a juggle state, attacks will increase the opponent's JC by this amount.

Airborne opponent at JC1 followed by attack with Juggle Increase value of 3 will set opponent to JC4

Juggle Limit (JL) : Property of an attack hitbox that determines whether it connects on a juggled opponent. The JL must be ≥ the opponent's JC to hit successfully.

An uppercut with a JL value of 5 will connect on an opponent at JC5 or below, but will whiff on JC6 opponent

Most normals have a JL value of 0, meaning they only work in Free Juggle (JC0) states

Some multi-hit attacks have different JL values on each hit, so a 3-hit move may only hit twice in juggles

An example to tie everything together:

An attack (JS3) launches opponent into the air (Opponent now at JC3)

Followed up with an attack (JI2/JL4); it connects, because JL4 ≥ JC3 (Opponent now at JC5)

Attempts to juggle again with same attack (JL4), but whiffs because JL4 < JC5 (Opponent hits the ground)

Drive Rush notes:

DR normals have a Juggle Start/Increase value of 0

DR normals have +3 added to their usual Juggle Limit

More recently, the official definitions used by Capcom are slightly different than these community-designated terms. When reading official patch notes, the following terms are used instead:

Combo Count Initial Value

Combo Count Additional Value

Combo Count Upper Limit

On Hit/Block

These are frame advantage values when the attack hits or is blocked. If the number is positive, then the move will recover before the defender can act again. If the number is negative, the defender will be able to act before the attacker and maybe even punish. KD refers to knockdown on hit, and the listed KD Advantage refers to how many frames the attacker can act before the defender finishes their wakeup animation.
Note that generally, there is an extra +2 hit advantage on Counterhits and +4 hit advantage on Punish Counters (exceptions are noted in the description).

Recovery

How many frames it takes for a move to finish after the active frames have finished. For projectiles, recovery is considered to begin after the first active frame.
Moves with different recovery values on hit/block/whiff may have multiple values listed like X(Y), with specific details listed in the description.

Startup

How many frames it takes before the move becomes 'active' or have a hit box. The last startup frame and the first active frame are the same frame, meaning all values are written as Startup + 1.
Moves with multiple relevant startup values may be listed as X(Y); for example, a move that hits airborne first before hitting grounded opponents, or a 2-hit move where the first hit whiffs at some ranges.

IASA / Actionable Recovery

Some moves play out an extended recovery animation when no other button/direction is input (for crouching moves, it applies when holding any down direction). These are often referred to as "actionable recovery" frames; in some games, the term IASA (Interruptible As Soon As) refers to the frame that Actionable Recovery begins.
Letting the Actionable Recovery frames play out can change the character's position, potentially setting up spacing traps by recovering farther away. For example, Manon 5HP will recover much farther away from the opponent if no input is performed immediately after her recovery; holding back or down-back to block will keep her much closer to the opponent.

An advancing poke that hits twice, allowing Mai to hitconfirm into light normals on hit. The first hit has a disjointed hitbox, making it hard to stuff in neutral. The follow-up link will work from a bit outside of 2MK range, with 2LP being more consistent (though 5LP can be more rewarding if you're a bit closer). She can't loop into it freely, but it's a good way to steal a turn when the opponent is expecting a tighter blockstring.

overview.title: Street Fighter 6/Elena
tables:
Giant Attacks: Some of the longest range normals in the game to control neutral with ease

Unique Mixups: Rolling can lead into high commitment but powerful setplay options that often end plus on block

Patience: Thrives with a slow, footsies style, getting big rewards from poking and whiff punishing

Stand/Crouch Confirms: Many moves that whiff on crouching opponents, forcing you to be mindful of your opponent's state

Poor Throw Loop: Needs to spend Drive gauge to perform throw loops, making her corner game weaker than most other characters

Burnout Victim: One of the unlucky few to have a non-invincible Level 1 Super, making Burnout checkmates more frequent

Standing Light Punch (5LP)

Standing Heavy Kick (5HK)

A[ L ~ L ~ L ]: 2LK ~ 2LP ~ H Scratch Wheel
On Block: stops at 2LP

Auto-hitconfirm if opponent is hit by the 2nd light in the string

Chaining into A[ 2L ] does not result in an alternate L Assist Combo (no longer automatically stops the combo when blocked)

A[ M ~ M ~ M ~ M ]: 2MP ~ OD Moon Glider ~ Follow-Up Launcher ~ SA2
On Block: stops at OD Moon Glider

Burnout: 2MP ~ L Moon Glider ~ Follow-Up Launcher

A[ H ~ H ~ H ~ H ~ H ~ H ~ H ~ H ]: 5MK ~ HK ~ OD Spinning Scythe ~ Lynx Whirl ~ Harvest Circle ~ L Rhino Horn ~ SA3
On Block: stops at 5MK ~ HK

Burnout: 5MK ~ HK ~ M Rhino Horn ~ SA3
Frame Data Tables / Hitbox Explanation - SF6

Red: Attack hitbox
Pink: Throw hitbox
Green: Hurtbox (strikes/projectiles)

Certain move properties, like Projectile Invuln or Air Invuln, may be printed onto the hurtbox and listed in the move description

A complete lack of hurtboxes represents full invulnerability

Blue: Throw hurtbox

Throw will succeed if the pink throw hitbox overlaps with the blue throwable hurtbox

Opponent must be on the ground (except for Air Throws which only target airborne opponents)

Teal: Unique/Interaction box

Applies character-specific effects when two of these hitboxes overlap

Examples: Rashid's air current, Blanka's electric moves + Blanka-chan, Guile's Sonic Blade + Sonic Boom

Purple: Armor/Counter Hitbox

Can appear on top of green hurtboxes or replace them entirely

Orange: Projectile Clash hitbox

Not a projectile itself, but interacts with and destroys projectiles of the same priority

Light Orange box on Drive Impact : represents the "cinematic DI Slowdown" interaction hitboxes

How many frames a move remains active (can hurt opponents) for. For projectiles with a maximum active period, a value may be listed in [brackets], but this number is not factored into the move's total frame count.
For multi-hit moves with no gaps between the active hitboxes, active frames are listed as X,Y (or sometimes X*Y)

For multi-hit moves with gaps between hits, active frames are listed as X(n)Y where n = the frame gap between hitboxes.

Available options for canceling one move into another move.
"Chn": Chain cancel (Light normals; specific chain options listed in Description)

"TC": Target Combo

"Sp": Special move

"SA": Super Art (if a number is listed, refers only to that specific Super; SA3 = Lv.3 Super Art)

"Jmp": Jump cancel (usually on hit only, if applicable)

"SS": Serenity Stream (Chun-Li's stance)

"PS": Prowler Stance (Alex's stance)
If one hit of a multi-hit attack is cancelable, this can be indicated with (1st), (2nd), etc.

Occasionally, a move can be canceled only into a specific follow-up (e.g. Dee Jay [4]6P > 22PP); this can be indicated by listing the move input in the Cancel field, or with an asterisk that is explained in the move notes (Sp*)

Hitconfirm reaction windows into Special Moves, Target Combos, and Super Arts.
Refers to the amount of time (in frames) you have to cancel one attack into another attack on reaction
e.g. most cancelable 2MKs have a 13 frame window to cancel into a Special/Super on reaction, making them nearly impossible to hitconfirm

Counts from the first frame the attack connects until the final cancelable frame
Visual effects like hitsparks and HP drain do not actually occur until frame 2; the first frame is still counted to keep the numbers consistent with previous games, and because it is technically possible to start reacting to the character's reeling animation on frame 1

If a Target Combo is cancelable into another attack, the hitconfirm window will include the entire sequence starting from the first hit
If there is a frame gap on block between hits of the TC, the hitconfirm window may also be included for just the followup hit

Some sequences like Ken's 5MP~HP TC may have a range of values listed (43f~47f). In this example, inputting 5MP~HP at its usual timing gives a 43f hitconfirm into a Special/Super. Delaying the chain into HP gives more total time for the final hitconfirm.

Attack damage on hit. Multi-hit moves may have the damage listed for individual hits as X,Y (or sometimes X*Y). Sometimes a move's damage changes depending on which active frame connects, or on cinematic vs. non-cinematic hits; in this case, multiple values may be listed, and it will be clarified in the move description.

Some moves cause additional damage scaling in combos. Refer to Game Data page for a more detailed breakdown.
Scaling Types:

Starter: When a move begins the combo , the next attack is scaled by X percent
e.g. Ryu 2MK (20% Starter) > Hadoken: Hadoken is at 80% damage scaling

Combo: When a move is comboed into , the next attack is scaled by X percent or X number of hits
e.g. Ryu 2HP > OD High Blade Kick (2-Hit Combo Scaling) > Shoryuken: Shoryuken is at 70% damage scaling (100% > 100% > [skip 80%] > 70%)

e.g. Cammy 5HP > OD Spiral Arrow (5% Combo Scaling) > Cannon Spike: Cannon Spike is at 75% damage scaling (100% > 100% > [80-5 = 75%])

Immediate: When a move is comboed into , this attack is scaled by X percent
e.g. Drive Impact Crumple (20% Starter) > Throw (20% Immediate): Throw is at 60% damage scaling

Multiplier: A damage scaling multiplier applies after Perfect Parry (50%) and mid-combo Drive Rush (15%). Any hits in the combo continue their usual damage scaling, but reduced by these amounts. These can bring the minimum scaling below the usual 10%, and they stack with each other; as a result, the minimum scaling can reach 4% using a long Drive Rush combo after Perfect Parry.

Minimum Scaling: The lowest damage scaling that can be applied to an attack. Super Art Level 1/2/3 generally has 30%/40%/50% minimum scaling respectively. This ensures the attack will still do reasonable damage even at the end of a heavily scaled combo.

Refers to the frame advantage when canceling a normal, command normal, or Target Combo into Drive Rush on hit or block (abbreviated as DRC for Drive Rush Cancel). This is calculated at the moment a follow-up attack can be input, not at the moment the character can block or perform movement options. An attack that with DRC +8 on Hit can link into an 8-frame attack, and DRC +4 on Block can create a true blockstring into a 4-frame attack.
Note that any DRC on Block worse than +4 cannot form a true blockstring, allowing the opponent to interrupt with an invincible reversal. Most light normals are slightly negative after a DRC on block, meaning the opponent can mash their fastest normal to guarantee a counter-hit (though this requires fast reactions). The attacking character could punish this with Light > DRC into an immediate invincible attack, but this would be an incredibly expensive and high-risk gambit.

Most airborne command normals, special moves, and Super Arts put the user in a "Forced Knockdown" state. While in this state, an air knockdown will occur when being hit by any attack, even if it would otherwise cause an air reset.
As an example, Ryu's 2HP causes an air reset when used as an anti-air. Against a move like Cammy's Hooligan Combination, however, the 2HP puts her into an air knockdown state. This allows Ryu to successfully cancel 2HP into Shoryuken for a juggle, similar to how a Drive Impact wall splat works. Taking advantage of Forced Knockdown juggles is important for dealing with moves like Ken's Dragonlash, Dhalsim's Air Teleport, or Kimberly's 6HK~Hop sequence.

Moves that already cause an air knockdown, like most j.MP air-to-airs, will not display the "Forced Knockdown" message.

Refers to the direction an attack must be blocked. L is for Low attacks (must be blocked crouching), H is for High attacks/overheads (must be blocked standing), LH is for attacks that can be blocked crouching or standing. T is for Throw attacks which cannot be blocked.

When a character is put into an Air Knockdown state, it is often possible to follow up with a Juggle attack before they hit the ground. In the simplest terms, there are 2 main juggle states:
Free Juggle: any attack can juggle, causing an Air Reset or an Air Knockdown

Limited Juggle: only specific attacks with juggle potential may juggle

The following is a more detailed overview of the SF6 juggle system:

Juggle Count (JC) : The status of the character being juggled. A high JC limits which attacks can work in juggles.

JC0: free juggle state - any attack that can hit an airborne opponent will work

JC1+: limited juggle state - juggle only works if the attack's Juggle Limit ≥ defender's Juggle Count
A juggle count of -1 represents a crumple state; this can lead to a grounded or airborne hit depending on timing

Juggle Start (JS) : When starting a juggle, the opponent's JC will be set to this value. May be different vs. standing and airborne opponents.

Attack with Juggle Start value of 3 will put opponent at JC3, so only attacks with Juggle Limit value ≥ 3 can follow up

Even for attacks that don't normally start a juggle, this is relevant for Forced Knockdown and Crumple situations

Juggle Increase (JI) : When opponent is already in a juggle state, attacks will increase the opponent's JC by this amount.

Airborne opponent at JC1 followed by attack with Juggle Increase value of 3 will set opponent to JC4

Juggle Limit (JL) : Property of an attack hitbox that determines whether it connects on a juggled opponent. The JL must be ≥ the opponent's JC to hit successfully.

An uppercut with a JL value of 5 will connect on an opponent at JC5 or below, but will whiff on JC6 opponent

Most normals have a JL value of 0, meaning they only work in Free Juggle (JC0) states

Some multi-hit attacks have different JL values on each hit, so a 3-hit move may only hit twice in juggles

An example to tie everything together:

An attack (JS3) launches opponent into the air (Opponent now at JC3)

Followed up with an attack (JI2/JL4); it connects, because JL4 ≥ JC3 (Opponent now at JC5)

Attempts to juggle again with same attack (JL4), but whiffs because JL4 < JC5 (Opponent hits the ground)

Drive Rush notes:

DR normals have a Juggle Start/Increase value of 0

DR normals have +3 added to their usual Juggle Limit

More recently, the official definitions used by Capcom are slightly different than these community-designated terms. When reading official patch notes, the following terms are used instead:

Combo Count Initial Value

Combo Count Additional Value

Combo Count Upper Limit

These are frame advantage values when the attack hits or is blocked. If the number is positive, then the move will recover before the defender can act again. If the number is negative, the defender will be able to act before the attacker and maybe even punish. KD refers to knockdown on hit, and the listed KD Advantage refers to how many frames the attacker can act before the defender finishes their wakeup animation.
Note that generally, there is an extra +2 hit advantage on Counterhits and +4 hit advantage on Punish Counters (exceptions are noted in the description).

How many frames it takes for a move to finish after the active frames have finished. For projectiles, recovery is considered to begin after the first active frame.
Moves with different recovery values on hit/block/whiff may have multiple values listed like X(Y), with specific details listed in the description.

How many frames it takes before the move becomes 'active' or have a hit box. The last startup frame and the first active frame are the same frame, meaning all values are written as Startup + 1.
Moves with multiple relevant startup values may be listed as X(Y); for example, a move that hits airborne first before hitting grounded opponents, or a 2-hit move where the first hit whiffs at some ranges.

Some moves play out an extended recovery animation when no other button/direction is input (for crouching moves, it applies when holding any down direction). These are often referred to as "actionable recovery" frames; in some games, the term IASA (Interruptible As Soon As) refers to the frame that Actionable Recovery begins.
Letting the Actionable Recovery frames play out can change the character's position, potentially setting up spacing traps by recovering farther away. For example, Manon 5HP will recover much farther away from the opponent if no input is performed immediately after her recovery; holding back or down-back to block will keep her much closer to the opponent.

Introduction

edit

A cheerful girl raised in the arms of the savannah, and a member of a clan of proud warriors. She has a talent for healing, and seeks to become a veterinarian.

Elena is a unique poking/counterpoking character, with an emphasis on powerful whiff punishes to back her up. She gets absurdly good reward out of playing “grounded footsies” Street Fighter is known for, dancing in and out of her effective range and encouraging her opponent to poke back. Once they stick out their feet a little too far forward, Elena pulls them into her offense and takes them straight to the corner. While Elena has several good pokes, she's much more balanced around encouraging an opponent to recklessly extend.

Elena brings with her a whole savannah plain of buttons that could dominate neutral if played well. Her bread and butter button is 5MK, a good poke, target-combo starter, and one of the few pokes in SF6 that's plus. 2MP is a long poke for checking drive rush and counter poking. If the opponent loves walking backwards and turtling, then 2MK, 2HK, and 3HK let Elena run them down. Crouching opponents can be opened up with her long-range 6MK, a quick overhead that leads to a small target combo and a knockdown. Elena is really good at checking opponents behavior, especially with her wide arsenal of target combos that can push her poking reward without using Drive.

Other than checking, she also excels at whiff punishing; being one of the characters that gets absurd reward for landing punish counter heavy buttons. 5HK and 5HP punish counter combos are devastating, crippling an opponent's health bar and dragging them to the corner like a raging elephant. Speaking of corner carry, “Rhino Horn” is a flying kick special move that lunges Elena forward. Almost all of her combos midscreen can end with this move, which gives great corner carry on hit. Outside of that, Elena also has “Scratch Wheel,” an anti-air DP, ”Moon Glide,” a backsway to bait pokes for a big counterhit, and “Spinning Scythe” for damage and decent okizeme.

Most essential to her gameplan is "Lynx Song" or "Roll". This causes Elena to roll along the ground, ducking under fireballs while charging up for a followup. If fully charged, each followup becomes very threatening; either she gets a plus on block meaty, a plus on block overhead, or a launcher. If you sense the opponent is going to retaliate, Elena can halt the roll and go for a bait or throw. Wake up with the wrong option, and Elena's strong punish routes will have your head spinning.

However, this meterless offense comes at a cost- Elena is very dependent on whiff punishes to get her gameplan started. While she has great ways to check the opponent, she lacks a lot of ways to enforce her own offense- her walkspeed is unremarkable when compared to other footsie-heavy characters, her Drive Rush is slow, and lacks fireballs to advance behind. As well, she is very dependent on Lynx Song to enforce her offense, which might he a turnoff to those who want a more traditional offensive kit. To sum it up, Elena is a beautiful and unique character to play. If you love characters that have good pokes, long buttons, and reward you for having rock solid fundamentals, then feel Elena's rhythm for yourself.

Pick if you like:
Avoid if you dislike:

Giant Attacks: Some of the longest range normals in the game to control neutral with ease

Unique Mixups: Rolling can lead into high commitment but powerful setplay options that often end plus on block

Patience: Thrives with a slow, footsies style, getting big rewards from poking and whiff punishing

Stand/Crouch Confirms: Many moves that whiff on crouching opponents, forcing you to be mindful of your opponent's state

Poor Throw Loop: Needs to spend Drive gauge to perform throw loops, making her corner game weaker than most other characters

Burnout Victim: One of the unlucky few to have a non-invincible Level 1 Super, making Burnout checkmates more frequent

Red: Attack hitbox
Pink: Throw hitbox
Green: Hurtbox (strikes/projectiles)

Certain move properties, like Projectile Invuln or Air Invuln, may be printed onto the hurtbox and listed in the move description

A complete lack of hurtboxes represents full invulnerability

Opponent must be on the ground (except for Air Throws which only target airborne opponents)

Applies character-specific effects when two of these hitboxes overlap

Examples: Rashid's air current, Blanka's electric moves + Blanka-chan, Guile's Sonic Blade + Sonic Boom

Can appear on top of green hurtboxes or replace them entirely

Not a projectile itself, but interacts with and destroys projectiles of the same priority

Active

How many frames a move remains active (can hurt opponents) for. For projectiles with a maximum active period, a value may be listed in [brackets], but this number is not factored into the move's total frame count.
For multi-hit moves with no gaps between the active hitboxes, active frames are listed as X,Y (or sometimes X*Y)

For multi-hit moves with gaps between hits, active frames are listed as X(n)Y where n = the frame gap between hitboxes.

Available options for canceling one move into another move.
"Chn": Chain cancel (Light normals; specific chain options listed in Description)

"TC": Target Combo

"Sp": Special move

"SA": Super Art (if a number is listed, refers only to that specific Super; SA3 = Lv.3 Super Art)

"SS": Serenity Stream (Chun-Li's stance)

If one hit of a multi-hit attack is cancelable, this can be indicated with (1st), (2nd), etc.

Refers to the amount of time (in frames) you have to cancel one attack into another attack on reaction

Visual effects like hitsparks and HP drain do not actually occur until frame 2; the first frame is still counted to keep the numbers consistent with previous games, and because it is technically possible to start reacting to the character's reeling animation on frame 1

If a Target Combo is cancelable into another attack, the hitconfirm window will include the entire sequence starting from the first hit
If there is a frame gap on block between hits of the TC, the hitconfirm window may also be included for just the followup hit

Sometimes a move's damage changes depending on which active frame connects, or on cinematic vs. non-cinematic hits; in this case, multiple values may be listed, and it will be clarified in the move description.

Some moves cause additional damage scaling in combos. Refer to Game Data page for a more detailed breakdown.

Starter: When a move begins the combo , the next attack is scaled by X percent
e.g. Ryu 2MK (20% Starter) > Hadoken: Hadoken is at 80% damage scaling

e.g. Ryu 2HP > OD High Blade Kick (2-Hit Combo Scaling) > Shoryuken: Shoryuken is at 70% damage scaling (100% > 100% > [skip 80%] > 70%)

e.g. Cammy 5HP > OD Spiral Arrow (5% Combo Scaling) > Cannon Spike: Cannon Spike is at 75% damage scaling (100% > 100% > [80-5 = 75%])

Immediate: When a move is comboed into , this attack is scaled by X percent
e.g. Drive Impact Crumple (20% Starter) > Throw (20% Immediate): Throw is at 60% damage scaling

The early active frames hit both standing and crouching, while the later active frames only hit standing opponents; this makes it a much easier whiff punish against standing pokes, even slightly outranging 2MK . Elena's 5HP is one of her best midrange starters. While it lacks the range and low crush properties of 5HK , the hitconfirmable Target Combo extension makes it far more rewarding to land. While crouching opponents cannot be hit by Elena's foot hitbox, crouchers have a wider hurtbox; this causes the "true" range to be almost identical against both standing and crouching. After confirming the hit into 5HP~HP , your juggle depends on how close Elena is to the opponent:

Close: 623HK , SA1 , SA3

Far: 2HK , 236KK , SA2

Landing this move as a Punish Counter makes it substantially stronger, as it allows the Target Combo extension to juggle higher than usual. It also makes the TC hitconfirm significantly easier; if you somehow miss the cancel window, Elena can still juggle after just the 5HP though the range is more restrictive. Landing this as a whiff punish can be difficult depending on the matchup, but some moves like Zangief's 5HP or Marisa's Gladius can be easily reacted to if you set up the correct spacing.

The hitbox has a large upward disjoint, making it a fairly consistent anti-air at longer ranges, though a bit slow to use on reaction. It can even work against neutral jumps if the opponent is trying to bait something like 6HP or Moon Glider . The opponent normally flips out of the air on hit, but if they use a Forced Knockdown move, the TC extension has a chance to juggle at least one hit; this leads to juggles much like the Punish Counter version.

One of the best 5-frame light normals in terms of range, giving Elena excellent punish and link options as well as a consistent Drive Rush check inside half screen. You can link into this button after 2LP in light chains, and can even be used as the 4th light in a combo when starting from point blank. It also combos after 5MK or Counter-hit 5MP / 2MK at closer ranges. Be careful not to use it on block at close range, as the opponent can punish with their own 4-frame normal.

5LK unfortunately cannot combo naturally into LK Spinning Scythe , instead relying on HK Scratch Wheel for consistency. If you can confirm the opponent is standing, you can also use LK / OD Rhino Horn for better corner carry and oki. When used as a Punish Counter , Elena gains a combo into OD Spinning Scythe , as well as MK Rhino Horn on standing characters.

A stubby pressure tool that, when followed with light normals, leads to frame traps on block or combos on hit, similar to Akuma's 5MP . 5LK is the most consistent combo follow-up, though it can whiff from farther out. On block, follow up with 2LP to keep the pressure tight; if you score a Counter-hit here, it can link to another 5MK from point blank or into 5LK from farther away. If you notice the opponent respects this pressure, you can try using multiple 5MKs in a sequence to harass their Drive gauge.

5MK is also important as Elena's fastest cancelable medium button, making it an important Drive Reversal punish and follow-up to several Counter-hit/Punish Counter starters. Convert punishes into a 5MP ~ MP Target Combo unless the opponent's move recovers in a crouching state (in which case, 2MP > 214MK / 623HK is a good replacement).

As an added bonus, this button leads to the 5MK ~ HK Target Combo, which gives her a consistent combo option even against crouching opponents while allowing a bailout with DRC on block.

A versatile and rewarding poke with incredible range, allowing Elena to chip safely at the opponent's Drive gauge. Its ability to crush low pokes makes it an extremely valuable tool in several matchups, making the usual " 2MK > DRC " gameplan much more risky to attempt against Elena.

While 5HK moves Elena forward, the active frames are actually stationary and the move cannot be spaced meaty for better frame advantage. Despite this, it's very easy to space safely against 4-frame lights, making its block disadvantage largely irrelevant. However, if you want to convert from Counter-hit 5HK in neutral, you may have to attack at a punishable range if the opponent has a solid 4-frame jab.

Elena's only 4-frame normal and her most important light combo tool. It chains with itself and 2LK for up to 3 hits, and can even link into 5LK as the 4th hit in a light string. Note that if you want to cancel into 214LK for oki, you should cancel directly from 2LP instead.

The range is above average, making it a better defensive option than most jabs; however, Elena lacks strong Counter-hit conversions outside of a close range link to 5MK . In most cases you have to stick with her underwhelming 5LK link. Confirming a light string into DRC~ 2LP grants a link to 2HP , though if you try this from a spaced raw DR Elena may still end up too far away.

Punishing the opponent's -4 attack allows Elena to link into 5MP , 2MK , or 2MP . The first two work at nearly any punish range and lead to a Target Combo for better damage (unless you're punishing a crouching attack). A crouching move like Kimberly's 3MK Slide should be punished with 2LP > 2MP instead.

Low Crush 14-24f (final active frame is considered standing but still has a high hurtbox); projectile invuln disappears for a brief period after Lynx Song (less effective as a fireball counter); projectile invuln does not apply to the top of Elena's head; Elena immediately loses crouch-sized hurtbox from Lynx Song; safe overhead that can lead to a 5MK combo after baiting the opponent's throw tech; puts airborne opponents into limited juggle state on hit (can always pick up corner juggles, but midscreen juggles depend on height/spacing); total minimum startup depends on which strength of Lynx Song was used (LP 16+22, MP 18+22, HP 19+22)

2 hits (if 1st hit is blocked, 2nd hit is no longer an overhead); Low Crush 5-22f (can avoid moves before becoming airborne); projectile invuln disappears for a brief period after Lynx Song/Whirl (less effective as a fireball counter); projectile invuln does not apply to the top of Elena's head; Elena immediately loses crouch-sized hurtbox from Lynx Song; overhead that gives strong follow-up pressure on block, a 2LP on hit, and a medium combo after baiting the opponent's low buttons or throw tech; puts airborne opponents into limited juggle state on hit (can always pick up a juggle, but exact route depends on height and distance); total minimum startup from OD Lynx Song is 18+22 (longer and variable when used from Lynx Whirl)

Forces stand; sways back slightly (can avoid attacks); sways on frames 5-14 (max distance of 0.40 on frame 5); puts airborne opponents into limited juggle state; safe option out of Drive Rush that can bait the opponent's button/throw and grants a light combo extension after a whiff punish

Forces stand; sways back a moderate distance (can avoid attacks); sways on frames 5-18 (max distance of 0.50 on frame 9); puts airborne opponents into limited juggle state; safe option out of Drive Rush that can bait the opponent's button/throw and grants a 5MK combo extension after a whiff punish

Forces stand; sways back significantly (can avoid attacks); sways on frames 5-23 (max distance of 0.71 on frames 14-16); puts airborne opponents into limited juggle state; safe option out of Drive Rush that can bait the opponent's button/throw and grants a 5MK combo extension after a whiff punish

Forces stand; sways back a moderate distance (can avoid attacks); sways on frames 5-19 (max distance of 0.56 on frame 9); puts airborne opponents into limited juggle state; safe option out of Drive Rush that can bait the opponent's button/throw and grants a light combo extension after a whiff punish
Hitconfirmable follow-up from safe sway starter; puts opponents into limited juggle state (into SA3)
Hitconfirmable follow-up from safe sway starter; puts opponents into limited juggle state (into SA2/SA3); sets up a safe jump vs. grounded opponents near the corner

Good anti-air with air invuln that fully covers the first 2 hits; cannot be used as an invincible reversal against grounded strikes/throws/projectiles (making it much more dangerous to be in Burnout); cannot hit cross-up; puts opponents into limited juggle state (can combo a 236KK full connect after a grounded hit); extreme block disadvantage allows many characters to set activate installs without sacrificing optimal punish starters

Excellent anti-fireball tool due to its invincibility and forward movement; slow startup makes it risky as a reversal (can be safely meatied by light normals); leaves Elena farther away than the Healing version, but with more advantage for Lynx Song or Drive Rush pressure; generally a poor anti-air but can catch some mid-range neutral jumps or divekick landing recovery; has a large combo-only hitbox that makes it more consistent in juggles; opponents can jump after the Super freeze to avoid a chip KO

Sacrifices damage and oki in exchange for healing 100 HP; the healing amount is not affected by damage scaling, making it more useful in a highly scaled combo; Elena builds 1 bar of Drive gauge when healing which also allows Drive regeneration to resume slightly earlier (also applies to Burnout gauge); excellent anti-fireball tool due to its invincibility and forward movement; slow startup makes it risky as a reversal (can be safely meatied by light normals); opponents can jump after the Super freeze to avoid a chip KO

Cinematic time regenerates ~2.1 Drive bars for Elena; large combo-only hitbox makes it more consistent in juggles; reliable but expensive reversal when in Burnout; very consistent anti-air at mid to long range, but cannot hit cross-up and can whiff under closer jumps; opponents cannot avoid a chip KO by jumping after the Super freeze

overview.title: Street Fighter 6/Sagat
tables:
Everything The Light Touches : Tricky projectile patterns, rewarding anti-airs, and massive pokes with confirmable knockdowns come together to give Sagat incredible space control, leaving no place on the screen truly safe.

Crippling Power : An array of pressure tools that can open up overly defensive opponents.

Court Juggler : Meterless launchers with plenty of options afterward, letting Sagat cash out his resources for huge damage and corner carry if he desires.

Moves One Space at a Time: Slower than average movement, often relying on Tiger Knee Crush or Drive Rush to move around

Uprisings and Downfalls: Conditioning your opponents to stand and crouch on demand to make your tools work to their fullest potential

No Bowing: Mediocre low options in pressure, and a throw that does not lead to a meterless throw loop

High Tiger Shot ( 2S / 3S )

Low Tiger Shot ( 1S )

A[ L ~ L ~ L ]: 2LK ~ 5LP ~ M Tiger Uppercut

Scaling Types:

Starter: When a move begins the combo , the next attack is scaled by X percent
e.g. Ryu 2MK (20% Starter) > Hadoken: Hadoken is at 80% damage scaling

Combo: When a move is comboed into , the next attack is scaled by X percent or X number of hits
e.g. Ryu 2HP > OD High Blade Kick (2-Hit Combo Scaling) > Shoryuken: Shoryuken is at 70% damage scaling (100% > 100% > [skip 80%] > 70%)

e.g. Drive Impact Crumple (20% Starter) > Throw (20% Immediate): Throw is at 60% damage scaling

Refers to the frame advantage when canceling a normal, command normal, or Target Combo into Drive Rush on hit or block (abbreviated as DRC for Drive Rush Cancel). This is calculated at the moment a follow-up attack can be input, not at the moment the character can block or perform movement options. An attack that with DRC +8 on Hit can link into an 8-frame attack, and DRC +4 on Block can create a true blockstring into a 4-frame attack.
Note that any DRC on Block worse than +4 cannot form a true blockstring, allowing the opponent to interrupt with an invincible reversal. Most light normals are slightly negative after a DRC on block, meaning the opponent can mash their fastest normal to guarantee a counter-hit (though this requires fast reactions). The attacking character could punish this with Light > DRC into an immediate invincible attack, but this would be an incredibly expensive and high-risk gambit.

This allows Ryu to successfully cancel 2HP into Shoryuken for a juggle, similar to how a Drive Impact wall splat works. Taking advantage of Forced Knockdown juggles is important for dealing with moves like Ken's Dragonlash, Dhalsim's Air Teleport, or Kimberly's 6HK~Hop sequence.

Moves that already cause an air knockdown, like most j.MP air-to-airs, will not display the "Forced Knockdown" message.

When a character is put into an Air Knockdown state, it is often possible to follow up with a Juggle attack before they hit the ground. In the simplest terms, there are 2 main juggle states:
Free Juggle: any attack can juggle, causing an Air Reset or an Air Knockdown

Limited Juggle: only specific attacks with juggle potential may juggle

The following is a more detailed overview of the SF6 juggle system:

Juggle Count (JC) : The status of the character being juggled. A high JC limits which attacks can work in juggles.

JC0: free juggle state - any attack that can hit an airborne opponent will work

JC1+: limited juggle state - juggle only works if the attack's Juggle Limit ≥ defender's Juggle Count
A juggle count of -1 represents a crumple state; this can lead to a grounded or airborne hit depending on timing

Juggle Start (JS) : When starting a juggle, the opponent's JC will be set to this value. May be different vs. standing and airborne opponents.

Attack with Juggle Start value of 3 will put opponent at JC3, so only attacks with Juggle Limit value ≥ 3 can follow up

Even for attacks that don't normally start a juggle, this is relevant for Forced Knockdown and Crumple situations

Juggle Increase (JI) : When opponent is already in a juggle state, attacks will increase the opponent's JC by this amount.

Airborne opponent at JC1 followed by attack with Juggle Increase value of 3 will set opponent to JC4

Juggle Limit (JL) : Property of an attack hitbox that determines whether it connects on a juggled opponent. The JL must be ≥ the opponent's JC to hit successfully.

An uppercut with a JL value of 5 will connect on an opponent at JC5 or below, but will whiff on JC6 opponent

Most normals have a JL value of 0, meaning they only work in Free Juggle (JC0) states

Some multi-hit attacks have different JL values on each hit, so a 3-hit move may only hit twice in juggles

An example to tie everything together:

An attack (JS3) launches opponent into the air (Opponent now at JC3)

Followed up with an attack (JI2/JL4); it connects, because JL4 ≥ JC3 (Opponent now at JC5)

Attempts to juggle again with same attack (JL4), but whiffs because JL4 < JC5 (Opponent hits the ground)

Drive Rush notes:

DR normals have a Juggle Start/Increase value of 0

DR normals have +3 added to their usual Juggle Limit

More recently, the official definitions used by Capcom are slightly different than these community-designated terms. When reading official patch notes, the following terms are used instead:

Combo Count Initial Value

Combo Count Additional Value

Combo Count Upper Limit

These are frame advantage values when the attack hits or is blocked. If the number is positive, then the move will recover before the defender can act again. If the number is negative, the defender will be able to act before the attacker and maybe even punish. KD refers to knockdown on hit, and the listed KD Advantage refers to how many frames the attacker can act before the defender finishes their wakeup animation.
Note that generally, there is an extra +2 hit advantage on Counterhits and +4 hit advantage on Punish Counters (exceptions are noted in the description).

How many frames it takes for a move to finish after the active frames have finished. For projectiles, recovery is considered to begin after the first active frame.
Moves with different recovery values on hit/block/whiff may have multiple values listed like X(Y), with specific details listed in the description.

How many frames it takes before the move becomes 'active' or have a hit box. The last startup frame and the first active frame are the same frame, meaning all values are written as Startup + 1.
Moves with multiple relevant startup values may be listed as X(Y); for example, a move that hits airborne first before hitting grounded opponents, or a 2-hit move where the first hit whiffs at some ranges.

These are often referred to as "actionable recovery" frames; in some games, the term IASA (Interruptible As Soon As) refers to the frame that Actionable Recovery begins.
Letting the Actionable Recovery frames play out can change the character's position, potentially setting up spacing traps by recovering farther away. For example, Manon 5HP will recover much farther away from the opponent if no input is performed immediately after her recovery; holding back or down-back to block will keep her much closer to the opponent.

Introduction

edit

The Emperor of Muay Thai. He was once one of the highest ranking members of Shadaloo, but has since left the criminal organization. He currently lives deep in the mountains, focusing only on his training.

In a reversal of his usual style, Sagat is a projectile zoner second and a brawler first with an emphasis on scary, safe pressure moves that make him a true titan up close. With excellent offensive and defensive tools, Sagat controls the screen with his superior battle prowess while giving up nothing when up close.

What you'll likely notice first about Sagat is his enormous frame. Easily the largest character on the roster , Sagat stands tall above his foes. This frame gives Sagat excellent poking normals, such as his 5HP , 5MK , and 2MK , all of which have ludicrous reach. Once Sagat has claimed the space in front of him as his own, he can begin layering in his strong zoning game. Sagat's signature move is his infamous Tiger Shot , fast projectiles that can be fired from either chest or knee height. Each version of Tiger Shot has its own purpose; the LP version forces opponents to block and prevents low-profile evasion, the MP version travels slower for lockdown zoning and midscreen juggle extensions, and the HP version is ludicrously fast and stuffs any opponent that tries to jump on reaction. Of course, tigers love to pounce on their prey, and Sagat is no different. Once the opponent is conditioned to sit still and duck under MP / HP Tiger Shot, Sagat can leap forward with Tiger Knee , an advancing knee strike that's plus against crouch block.

If allowed to close the distance, Sagat has a number of excellent pressure options to rip his opponent to shreds. His 5MP is +2 , MP Tiger Shot is plus if stand blocked, 6HK leaves him at +4 on stand block, and Tiger Knee can be spaced for frame advantage as well. Most terrifying of all is Sagat's new special Tiger Nexus , a Rekka-like move similar to Ken's Jinrai Kick. Upon hitting the opponent, Sagat can follow up with three options. The 6LK ender is an overhead that frame traps on block and knocks down on Counter-hit , the 6MK ender knocks down and give amazing block advantage but whiffs on crouchers, and the 6HK ender gives a full juggle launch anywhere on-screen while remaining plus on block, but has slow interruptible startup. Mixing between the various follow-ups forces opponents to decide whether they want to mitigate any potential damage, or prevent Sagat from scoring endless plus frames to drain their Drive gauge.

Speaking of juggles, Sagat has some of the best corner carry in the game, with 6HK , Tiger Knee , and Tiger Uppercut all functioning as extremely far traveling combo extenders/enders, allowing Sagat to quickly corner and pressure opponents.
Another one of his most important combo moves is Tiger Monolith ( 4HP ), a reliable anti air normal that also grants extremely high damage combos and gives him some big launches from Nova. This move also lets Sagat reliably combo into charged hp uppercut, which can quickly obliterate enemy health at the cost of worse okizeme.

Sagat boasts high damage whenever he lands a clean hit. He can spend Drive meter in a plethora of ways, including OD High Tiger Shot which juggles into Level 1 Super anywhere on screen. He has two meterless launchers in 4HP and Nova Tiger , both of which grant amazing corner carry with as little as 1 additional Drive bar. Sagat's Level 2 Super has four different follow-ups based on the direction held, giving him the option to pursue damage/corner carry, oki, a side swap, or a juggle launcher that lets Sagat dump additional resources to get the best of all worlds. All of this leads to an offense truly fit for a king, with exceptional reward once Sagat finds a hit.

However, as implied before, Sagat is sorely lacking in threatening lows for offense . While his 2LK can begin a light chain as is the standard, his movement speed and relatively poor midscreen oki makes it difficult to convert properly, it also makes neutral difficult if solely relying on buttons since most opponents will be faster than him which can lead to whiff punishers having a field day with Sagat if poorly conditioned. 2MK is not special cancelable, and does a poor job of maintaining Drive Rush momentum to initiate pressure, and while 6LK is a good standing low, it is fairly reactable and only grants links with Counter-hit , Drive Rush , or meaty timing. Crouching opponents can avoid many of Sagat's strongest tools, including MP / HP Tiger Shot, 6HK , and Greedy Tiger . Sagat must encourage opponents to stand by poking with lows to the best of his ability, and by threatening from a distance with Tiger Knee. Sagat is generally very committal , with slow movement, expensive throw loops, slow reversals, and slow Super Arts , with plenty of ways to punish him if he isn't cautious. Sagat's strong offense requires equally strong foresight from the player. If you like big normals, calculated zoning, excellent pressure, and Muay Thai in general, Sagat will show you how to become a true king.

Pick if you like:
Avoid if you dislike:

Everything The Light Touches : Tricky projectile patterns, rewarding anti-airs, and massive pokes with confirmable knockdowns come together to give Sagat incredible space control, leaving no place on the screen truly safe.

Crippling Power : An array of pressure tools that can open up overly defensive opponents.

Court Juggler : Meterless launchers with plenty of options afterward, letting Sagat cash out his resources for huge damage and corner carry if he desires.

Moves One Space at a Time: Slower than average movement, often relying on Tiger Knee Crush or Drive Rush to move around

Uprisings and Downfalls: Conditioning your opponents to stand and crouch on demand to make your tools work to their fullest potential

No Bowing: Mediocre low options in pressure, and a throw that does not lead to a meterless throw loop

Juggles

When a character is put into an Air Knockdown state, it is often possible to follow up with a Juggle attack before they hit the ground. In the simplest terms, there are 2 main juggle states:
Free Juggle: any attack can juggle, causing an Air Reset or an Air Knockdown

Limited Juggle: only specific attacks with juggle potential may juggle

The following is a more detailed overview of the SF6 juggle system:

Juggle Count (JC) : The status of the character being juggled. A high JC limits which attacks can work in juggles.

JC0: free juggle state - any attack that can hit an airborne opponent will work

JC1+: limited juggle state - juggle only works if the attack's Juggle Limit ≥ defender's Juggle Count
A juggle count of -1 represents a crumple state; this can lead to a grounded or airborne hit depending on timing

Juggle Start (JS) : When starting a juggle, the opponent's JC will be set to this value. May be different vs. standing and airborne opponents.

Attack with Juggle Start value of 3 will put opponent at JC3, so only attacks with Juggle Limit value ≥ 3 can follow up

Even for attacks that don't normally start a juggle, this is relevant for Forced Knockdown and Crumple situations

Juggle Increase (JI) : When opponent is already in a juggle state, attacks will increase the opponent's JC by this amount.

Airborne opponent at JC1 followed by attack with Juggle Increase value of 3 will set opponent to JC4

Juggle Limit (JL) : Property of an attack hitbox that determines whether it connects on a juggled opponent. The JL must be ≥ the opponent's JC to hit successfully.

An uppercut with a JL value of 5 will connect on an opponent at JC5 or below, but will whiff on JC6 opponent

Most normals have a JL value of 0, meaning they only work in Free Juggle (JC0) states

Some multi-hit attacks have different JL values on each hit, so a 3-hit move may only hit twice in juggles

An example to tie everything together:

An attack (JS3) launches opponent into the air (Opponent now at JC3)

Followed up with an attack (JI2/JL4); it connects, because JL4 ≥ JC3 (Opponent now at JC5)

Attempts to juggle again with same attack (JL4), but whiffs because JL4 < JC5 (Opponent hits the ground)

Drive Rush notes:

DR normals have a Juggle Start/Increase value of 0

DR normals have +3 added to their usual Juggle Limit

More recently, the official definitions used by Capcom are slightly different than these community-designated terms. When reading official patch notes, the following terms are used instead:

Combo Count Initial Value

Combo Count Additional Value

Combo Count Upper Limit

On Hit/Block

These are frame advantage values when the attack hits or is blocked. If the number is positive, then the move will recover before the defender can act again. If the number is negative, the defender will be able to act before the attacker and maybe even punish. KD refers to knockdown on hit, and the listed KD Advantage refers to how many frames the attacker can act before the defender finishes their wakeup animation.
Note that generally, there is an extra +2 hit advantage on Counterhits and +4 hit advantage on Punish Counters (exceptions are noted in the description).

Recovery

How many frames it takes for a move to finish after the active frames have finished. For projectiles, recovery is considered to begin after the first active frame.
Moves with different recovery values on hit/block/whiff may have multiple values listed like X(Y), with specific details listed in the description.

Startup

How many frames it takes before the move becomes 'active' or have a hit box. The last startup frame and the first active frame are the same frame, meaning all values are written as Startup + 1.
Moves with multiple relevant startup values may be listed as X(Y); for example, a move that hits airborne first before hitting grounded opponents, or a 2-hit move where the first hit whiffs at some ranges.

IASA / Actionable Recovery

Some moves play out an extended recovery animation when no other button/direction is input (for crouching moves, it applies when holding any down direction). These are often referred to as "actionable recovery" frames; in some games, the term IASA (Interruptible As Soon As) refers to the frame that Actionable Recovery begins.
Letting the Actionable Recovery frames play out can change the character's position, potentially setting up spacing traps by recovering farther away. For example, Manon 5HP will recover much farther away from the opponent if no input is performed immediately after her recovery; holding back or down-back to block will keep her much closer to the opponent.

A chainable and cancelable jab, allowing Sagat to convert light chains at a range most characters cannot. This is especially important for Sagat, as all his light normals have massive pushback. This makes it weak for setting up tick throws or Counter-hit pressure strings, but excellent for keeping him out of the opponent's poke range after a 3-light string.

5LP is Sagat's only light normal that combos naturally into LK Tiger Nexus , but only after 2 lights from close range. Cancel into MP Tiger Uppercut at longer ranges and after a 3-light chain.

As his primary 5f punish tool, its range is solid but noticeably shorter than most shoto 5LKs . Its high pushback also leaves him out of range to link into 5LK or 2MP when punishing key moves like M. Bison's LK Scissor Kick or Ken's Jinrai~Low . The most consistent punish option is simply a cancel into HP Tiger Uppercut or MK Tiger Nexus ~ Greedy Tiger . Spending more resources can lead to better corner carry or oki, but not much damage.

A short-ranged pressure starter and Sagat's only plus-on-block button that hits crouching opponents. Frame trapping into itself will lead to a trade against 4f jabs, usually resulting in a link to 5LK (and often 2MP depending on the pushback). The pushback is so high that Sagat cannot tick throw without walking forward, which is risky considering his slow walk speed. Drive Rush momentum will keep him in throw range, but the block advantage is so high that the throw must be delayed at least 2 frames. This also forms a true blockstring into another 5MP , which is good for dealing safe Drive damage but cannot be a frame trap without delaying the button.

With 4 active frames, 5MP is a great meaty tool that can even be safe to Drive Reversal with good timing. Meaty timing can add up to +3 frames of advantage (+7 if used from Drive Rush ) with the right setup.

On hit, Sagat has no cancel options, but he can link into itself and end with 5LP > MP Tiger Uppercut for solid damage and a knockdown. On Counter-hit , you'll usually link into 2MP for consistency, but 4HP is also possible at close range; one blocked 5MP into CH 5MP is too far for this link without Drive Rush momentum.

5MP is one of Sagat's most important punish starters despite its stubby range, as it links into 5HK to force stand and combo into HK Tiger Nexus . This is especially important against blocked Drive Reversal ; he can get over 3000 meterless damage or 3500 1-bar damage from PC 5MP , while barely cracking 2000 on a jab or throw punish (sorry, Modern players).

One notable weakness of 5MP is its overlapping input with his 6MP Overhead , making it harder to walk forward and stagger his block pressure. Being careful to let go of the forward direction can cause players to waste a frame or two, allowing opponents to interrupt with delayed buttons that might otherwise have been too late.

A long range light poke; much like Zangief's 5LK , its startup and recovery are more akin to a medium normal. Unlike Zangief, this button is very unrewarding when canceled into Drive Rush , as it gives no true pressure on block and cannot combo naturally on hit. As a whiff punish starter, 5LK > DRC can combo into 2MP for a bit more damage.

The range on 5LK is slightly longer than 2MP , making it a more consistent link in some +7~8 scenarios. Its only real hitconfirm cancel ender is MP Tiger Uppercut , as other cancels are either too slow or whiff on crouching at most ranges. From farther ranges, you can buffer HP Tiger Uppercut as a whiff punish ender, which will easily combo on Counter-hit/Punish Counter with its gargantuan range.

Like 5MP , this button has input overlap with a command normal ( 6LK ) that makes it harder to perform while walking forward. This input overlap is much less impactful, but can make it a little harder to walk forward and whiff punish consistently.
